questions.stem: The role of human resource management is best described as:
options: managing the employment relationship so that staff help achieve business goals
managing the transformation of inputs into goods and services for customers
managing the business's cash, assets and liabilities so that it stays solvent and liquid
managing the marketing mix to meet the needs of the target market
questions.explanation: Human resource management covers acquiring, developing, rewarding and separating staff so the workforce supports the business's objectives. Transforming inputs is operations, and managing cash and assets is finance.

questions.stem: Building human capital refers to:
options: raising money from shareholders to fund business growth
reducing the number of managers in the organisation
increasing the skills, knowledge and experience of the workforce
buying new equipment so that fewer employees are needed in production
questions.explanation: Human capital is the value of employees' skills, knowledge and experience, built through training, development and careful recruitment. Buying equipment adds physical capital, not human capital.

questions.stem: A Newcastle call centre surveys staff and finds they feel committed, enthusiastic and willing to go beyond their basic duties. Which HR objective does this measure?
options: capacity utilisation
employee engagement
labour cost efficiency
building human capital
questions.explanation: Employee engagement is employees' emotional commitment to their work and the business, shown in discretionary effort. Labour cost efficiency is about getting more output for each dollar spent on labour.

questions.stem: A retailer cuts training and replaces many experienced staff with lower-paid casuals. Labour costs fall 12%, but customer complaints rise. Which conflict between HR objectives does this show?
options: labour cost efficiency was pursued at the expense of human capital and engagement
employee engagement was pursued at the expense of labour cost efficiency
building human capital was pursued at the expense of employee engagement
there is no conflict, because lower labour costs always improve service
questions.explanation: Cutting labour costs met the efficiency objective, but losing skilled staff and training reduced human capital, and engagement and service suffered. HR objectives can conflict and must be balanced.

questions.stem: In human resource management, the role of a line manager is to:
options: supervise employees day to day and put HR policies into practice
represent employees in collective negotiations with the employer over pay
approve enterprise agreements and settle industrial disputes
provide services to the business under a commercial contract
questions.explanation: Line managers directly supervise staff and carry out many HR tasks, such as rostering, on-the-job training and performance feedback. Representing employees is a union role, and approving agreements is the Fair Work Commission's role.

questions.stem: A Wollongong builder engages an electrician who uses her own tools, works for several clients and sends an invoice for each job. She is most likely:
options: a line manager of the builder
an independent contractor
a permanent part-time employee
a casual employee of the builder
questions.explanation: Independent contractors run their own business, control how they work, often use their own equipment and invoice for results. Employees work in the employer's business under its direction and are paid wages.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage for a business of using contractors rather than employees for specialist work?
options: lower hourly rates, because contractors are always paid less than employees
flexibility to buy skills only when needed, without employee entitlements such as paid leave
greater control over how and when the work is carried out each day
stronger loyalty and engagement, because contractors fully share the business's culture and values
questions.explanation: Contractors give access to specialist skills for a set job, and the business does not provide employee entitlements such as paid leave. In return it has less control, and contractors' rates are often higher per hour.

questions.stem: Which is a role of trade unions in the employment relationship?
options: setting the national minimum wage for all employees in Australia each year
recruiting and selecting employees on behalf of businesses
deciding whether a business's enterprise agreement is approved
representing members and bargaining collectively on pay and conditions
questions.explanation: Trade unions are organisations of employees that represent their members, negotiate enterprise agreements and campaign for better pay, conditions and safety. Setting the minimum wage and approving agreements are roles of the Fair Work Commission.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the role of employees in human resource management?
options: they supply labour and skills, follow lawful directions and contribute to workplace goals
they set the business's HR policies and decide what all staff members will be paid
they approve enterprise agreements on behalf of the Fair Work Commission
they provide services as separate businesses and invoice for each completed job
questions.explanation: Employees provide their skills and effort in return for wages and conditions, and must follow lawful, reasonable directions and work safely. Running a separate business and invoicing describes contractors.

questions.stem: Which is the main benefit of effective recruitment and selection?
options: allowing the business to pay new employees less than the award rate
hiring people who perform well and stay, reducing turnover and rehiring costs
removing the need for any induction or training of new employees
guaranteeing that every new employee will be promoted within a year
questions.explanation: Choosing the right people raises productivity and engagement and lowers the costs of poor performance, turnover and repeated hiring. Even well-chosen staff need induction and training, and award rates must still be paid.

questions.stem: Communication, teamwork and problem-solving are examples of:
options: cultural fit
soft skills
technical skills
job fit
questions.explanation: Soft skills are interpersonal and personal abilities used in any role. Technical skills are job-specific abilities, such as operating machinery or using accounting software.

questions.stem: A Sydney engineering firm needs a structural engineer who can use specialised design software. Which recruitment requirement does this describe?
options: technical skills
soft skills
cultural fit
global recruitment
questions.explanation: Technical skills are the specific knowledge and abilities needed to perform a job's tasks, such as using design software. Soft skills, such as communication, apply across roles.

questions.stem: An applicant has excellent qualifications, but the business values close teamwork and she prefers working alone. The concern is about:
options: cultural fit, the match between her values and the business's culture
job fit, the match between her qualifications and the tasks the job requires
technical skills, the specialised abilities needed for the role
soft skills, the abilities that are taught in off-the-job training
questions.explanation: Cultural fit is how well a person's values and working style suit the organisation's culture. Her qualifications suggest good job fit; the concern is how she would work within the team.

questions.stem: A business hires only applicants who 'feel like us' to protect its cultural fit. Which is the main risk of this approach?
options: it forces the business to recruit only through internal promotions
it can reduce diversity and lead to bias against capable applicants
it guarantees that new staff will lack the technical skills required
it makes recruitment unlawful in every case, regardless of the reasons
questions.explanation: Overemphasising cultural fit can become a cover for hiring people with similar backgrounds, reducing diversity and possibly breaching anti-discrimination law. Fit is best judged against stated values, alongside skills and job fit.

questions.stem: Which is an example of internal recruitment?
options: advertising a vacant role on a popular online job board
using a recruitment agency to find a new accountant
attending a university careers fair to find graduates
promoting a team leader to fill a vacant supervisor role
questions.explanation: Internal recruitment fills a vacancy from existing staff, through promotion or transfer. Job boards, agencies and careers fairs reach people outside the business.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of internal recruitment?
options: it is quicker and cheaper, and the candidate already knows the business
it brings new ideas and skills that the business does not already have
it gives access to the largest possible pool of applicants for the role
it never leaves another vacancy that must also be filled by the business
questions.explanation: Internal candidates are known to the business, need less induction and are cheaper to recruit, and promotion can motivate staff. New ideas and a larger pool are advantages of external recruitment.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of internal recruitment?
options: a limited pool of candidates and fewer fresh ideas entering the business
a long and expensive search using agencies and paid job advertisements
a new employee who does not know the business's systems or culture
a greater risk of hiring someone whose work history is completely unknown
questions.explanation: Recruiting from within limits choice to existing staff and can cause stagnant thinking and resentment among unsuccessful colleagues. Costly searches and unfamiliar new staff are drawbacks of external recruitment.

questions.stem: A struggling Dubbo manufacturer needs a new operations manager to modernise outdated processes. No current staff have experience with modern systems. Which recruitment choice is best justified?
options: internal recruitment, because current staff know the outdated processes well
no recruitment, because development of existing staff is never too slow
external recruitment, to bring in skills and new ideas the business lacks
internal recruitment, because it always costs less than any external search
questions.explanation: When the business needs skills and fresh thinking that do not exist internally, external recruitment is justified despite higher cost and induction time. Knowledge of the old processes does not meet the need to modernise.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of global recruitment?
options: no legal requirements, because overseas workers are not employees
access to skills that are scarce in the local labour market
lower recruitment costs than hiring from within the business
no need for induction, because overseas staff already know the business
questions.explanation: Recruiting from overseas widens the talent pool and can fill skill shortages and bring international experience. It is usually costlier and slower than local hiring.

questions.stem: A regional NSW hospital recruits nurses from overseas to fill vacancies. Which is a disadvantage it is most likely to face?
options: a smaller pool of candidates than if it recruited only within its own local region
fewer skills in the workforce because overseas nurses never hold recognised nursing qualifications
a ban on employing anyone who was not born in Australia in a public hospital
visa sponsorship costs, longer lead times, and recognition of overseas qualifications
questions.explanation: Global recruitment often involves visa costs and paperwork, delays, checking whether overseas qualifications meet Australian registration standards, and support for relocation. It widens rather than narrows the candidate pool.

questions.stem: Which is a selection method?
options: careers fairs
internal promotion
reference checks
job advertisements
questions.explanation: Selection methods choose between applicants: résumé screening, interviews, tests and reference checks. Advertisements and careers fairs are ways to attract applicants, which is recruitment.

questions.stem: A national retailer receives 2,000 applications for 40 roles and uses software to filter résumés for required qualifications. Which is the main limitation of this screening method?
options: it is slower and more expensive than reading every résumé by hand
it can be used only after interviews have been completed for every applicant
it guarantees that every shortlisted applicant will be a good cultural fit for the retailer
suitable applicants may be rejected because their résumés use different keywords
questions.explanation: Automated résumé screening saves time with large volumes, but rigid keyword filters can miss strong candidates and may reflect bias in how the tool was designed. Screening happens before interviews, not after.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of interviews as a selection method?
options: they cannot be used to assess an applicant's cultural fit at all
they can be carried out only by an external recruitment agency
interviewers' first impressions and biases can influence their decisions
they give no information about an applicant's communication skills
questions.explanation: Interviews reveal communication skills and fit, but judgements can be subjective. Structured interviews, with the same questions and scoring for every applicant, reduce bias.

questions.stem: Applicants for a forklift driver role at a Penrith warehouse must complete a supervised driving task. This selection test assesses:
options: the applicant's personality type and preferred working style
the accuracy of the applicant's past employment history
the applicant's knowledge of the business's history
the applicant's practical ability to perform the job
questions.explanation: Skills or work-sample tests show directly whether an applicant can do key tasks of the job. Personality tests assess working style, and reference checks verify past employment.

questions.stem: Which selection method is best used to verify claims an applicant has made about past performance?
options: a psychometric test of personality traits
an unstructured interview with the applicant
an automated keyword screen of the résumé
reference checks with former supervisors
questions.explanation: Reference checks gather evidence from people who have supervised the applicant, confirming work history and performance. Interviews and résumés rely on the applicant's own account, and personality tests do not verify past performance.

questions.stem: Which is a benefit of human resource development?
options: lower wages, because trained staff earn less
a more skilled, adaptable and engaged workforce
a guaranteed reduction in the number of employees
the removal of the need to recruit any new staff
questions.explanation: Development builds human capital, improves productivity and quality, helps staff adapt to change and can raise engagement and retention. It does not remove the need to recruit.

questions.stem: Induction is best described as:
options: training experienced employees to use a new piece of specialised equipment
assessing employees' performance against their goals at the end of each year
pairing a senior employee with a junior one for long-term career guidance
introducing new employees to the business, their role, colleagues and safety rules
questions.explanation: Induction helps new staff settle in quickly and safely by explaining the business, its policies, their role and WHS procedures. Long-term guidance from a senior colleague is mentoring.

questions.stem: A new apprentice at a Tamworth engineering workshop learns to weld by working alongside an experienced tradesperson. This is:
options: off-the-job training
induction
résumé screening
on-the-job training
questions.explanation: On-the-job training happens in the workplace while doing the job, often guided by an experienced colleague. Off-the-job training happens away from the work area, such as at TAFE.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of off-the-job training?
options: expert instruction without the distractions of normal work
no lost production while the employee is being trained
training is always cheaper than learning on the job
skills are learnt in exactly the employee's own workplace
questions.explanation: Off-the-job courses offer specialist trainers and focused learning, and may lead to formal qualifications. Their drawbacks are cost, time away from work and skills that may not transfer perfectly to the workplace.

questions.stem: A manager meets each staff member every fortnight to discuss what is going well and what to improve. Which development method is this?
options: mentoring
induction
off-the-job training
feedback
questions.explanation: Regular feedback tells employees how they are performing and how to improve, supporting development continuously. Mentoring is a longer-term relationship with an experienced colleague focused on career growth.

questions.stem: A law firm pairs each junior lawyer with a senior partner who gives career advice and shares experience over several years. Which statement best evaluates this method?
options: mentoring is the quickest way to teach a specific technical task to a new employee
mentoring replaces the need for any induction when junior lawyers first join
mentoring is a form of off-the-job training delivered at a university campus
mentoring builds skills and retention, but depends on the mentor's time and commitment
questions.explanation: Mentoring passes on experience and supports long-term development and retention, but it takes senior staff time and relies on a good match. For a specific task, on-the-job training is quicker.

questions.stem: Unemployment in NSW rises during a recession. What is the most likely effect on a business's recruitment?
options: much higher wages are needed to attract any applicants at all
employees are more likely to resign and look for other jobs
more applicants for each vacancy, making suitable staff easier to find
fewer applicants for each vacancy, making suitable staff harder to find
questions.explanation: When unemployment is high, more people compete for each job, so recruitment is easier and wage pressure eases. Staff are also less likely to resign because other jobs are scarce.

questions.stem: During a strong economic boom with low unemployment, which HR challenge is most likely?
options: a flood of applicants for every vacancy
pressure to make many staff redundant
falling wages across the labour market
difficulty attracting and keeping skilled staff
questions.explanation: In a boom, labour is in short supply, so businesses compete for workers, wages rise and turnover increases. Redundancies and many applicants are more typical of a downturn.

questions.stem: A Sydney bank introduces AI chatbots that handle routine customer questions. What is the most likely effect on its labour needs?
options: fewer staff for routine enquiries, but more need for technology and complex-service skills
more staff for routine enquiries, and much less need for any technology or digital skills
no change to labour needs, because technology does not affect jobs
the business must stop all recruitment, as AI will replace every role
questions.explanation: Technology can automate routine tasks, reducing some roles while creating demand for staff who manage the technology and handle complex cases. This often requires retraining existing staff.

questions.stem: A business moves leave requests, rostering and payslips onto a cloud-based HR system that staff access on their phones. Which is the main benefit?
options: the removal of all legal obligations on employee records
a guaranteed rise in every employee's level of engagement
no further need for the business to protect employee data
faster, more accurate HR administration with less paperwork
questions.explanation: Digital HR systems automate routine administration, reduce errors and give staff self-service access. The business must still keep accurate records and protect personal information.

questions.stem: A Parramatta company builds a workforce from many cultural backgrounds and trains all staff in cultural capability. Which is the strongest business benefit?
options: a guarantee that conflict between employees will never arise in the business
a wider range of ideas and a better understanding of a diverse customer base
lower wage costs, because diverse employees are paid less than other employees
an exemption from anti-discrimination laws for the business and its managers
questions.explanation: Diverse, inclusive teams bring varied perspectives that can improve decisions and innovation and help the business serve diverse customers. Cultural capability training helps staff work respectfully together, though it cannot guarantee there will be no conflict.

questions.stem: To cut costs, an HR manager replaces formal training with on-the-job learning only. Within a year, product defects rise and operations misses its quality targets. What does this best show?
options: training costs can always be cut without any effect on other business functions
HR decisions are interdependent with operations and must align with business strategy
on-the-job training is always ineffective and should never be used by businesses
operations is solely responsible for product quality, so HR decisions have no effect on it
questions.explanation: Cutting development reduced workers' skills, which affected operations' quality objectives. HR decisions must be aligned across functions and with strategy. On-the-job training is useful, but not always sufficient on its own.
